title: The Poisson Process

intro.x: The Poisson process models events that occur at random moments in continuous time: customer arrivals, radioactive decays, insurance claims, packets at a router. It combines two earlier ideas, the Poisson distribution (counts) and the exponential distribution (waiting times), and gives a single object with several equivalent descriptions. We derive each description and the main properties: superposition, thinning, the uniformity of arrival times, and the inspection paradox.

blocks.x: A counting process $(N(t))_{t\ge0}$ has $N(0)=0$, takes non-negative integer values, and is non-decreasing and right-continuous with jumps of size $1$. $N(t)$ is the number of events in $(0,t]$. The arrival times are $T_n=\inf\{t:N(t)\ge n\}$ and the interarrival times are $\tau_n=T_n-T_{n-1}$ ($T_0=0$).
A counting process $N$ is a Poisson process with rate $\lambda>0$ if
(independent increments) for $0\le t_0
(Poisson increments) $N(t)-N(s)\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))$ for $s
The next three results show that this definition is equivalent to two others that are easier to verify in applications.
Let $N$ be a counting process with independent and stationary increments (the distribution of $N(t+h)-N(t)$ depends only on $h$) such that, as $h\downarrow0$,
\Prob(N(h)=1)=\lambda h+o(h),\qquad\Prob(N(h)\ge2)=o(h).
Then $N$ is a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$.
Let $P_n(t)=\Prob(N(t)=n)$. For $n=0$: by independence and stationarity of increments, $P_0(t+h)=P_0(t)P_0(h)$ and $P_0(h)=1-\lambda h+o(h)$, so
\frac{P_0(t+h)-P_0(t)}h=P_0(t)\frac{P_0(h)-1}h\to-\lambda P_0(t),
i.e. $P_0'=-\lambda P_0$ with $P_0(0)=1$, whence $P_0(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$. For $n\ge1$, conditioning on $N(t)$ and the increment over $(t,t+h]$,
P_n(t+h)=P_n(t)P_0(h)+P_{n-1}(t)\Prob(N(h)=1)+\sum_{j\ge2}P_{n-j}(t)\Prob(N(h)=j),

and the last sum is at most $\Prob(N(h)\ge2)=o(h)$. Therefore $P_n'(t)=-\lambda P_n(t)+\lambda P_{n-1}(t)$, $P_n(0)=0$. Put $Q_n(t)=e^{\lambda t}P_n(t)$; then $Q_n'=\lambda Q_{n-1}$, $Q_0\equiv1$, and induction gives $Q_n(t)=(\lambda t)^n/n!$. So $P_n(t)=e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^n/n!$: $N(t)\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda t)$. By stationarity the same holds for any increment of length $t-s$.
A counting process whose interarrival times $\tau_1,\tau_2,\dots$ are i.i.d. $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ has $N(t)\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda t)$ for every $t$ (and is a Poisson process).

We prove the marginal statement. $T_n=\tau_1+\dots+\tau_n\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(n,\lambda)$ (Theorem 8.7) and $\{N(t)\ge n\}=\{T_n\le t\}$. Let $G_n(t)=\Prob(T_n\le t)=\int_0^t\frac{\lambda^nx^{n-1}e^{-\lambda x}}{(n-1)!}dx$. We claim $G_n(t)=\sum_{k\ge n}e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k/k!$. Both sides vanish at $t=0$ and have the same derivative: differentiating the series,

(a telescoping sum), which is the Gamma density. Hence $\Prob(N(t)\ge n)=\sum_{k\ge n}e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k/k!$ for all $n$, and subtracting consecutive tails gives $\Prob(N(t)=n)=e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^n/n!$. (Independence of increments follows from the memorylessness of the exponential: at any time the future interarrival times are independent of the past and again i.i.d. Exp$(\lambda)$.)

Conversely, in a Poisson process the interarrival times are i.i.d. Exp$(\lambda)$: the first arrival satisfies $\Prob(\tau_1>t)=\Prob(N(t)=0)=e^{-\lambda t}$, and by independent and stationary increments the process restarts afresh at each arrival.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: three views of the same object

blocks.x: Poisson process $\iff$ i.i.d. exponential gaps $\iff$ independent, stationary, and “rare, one at a time” increments. Memorylessness of the exponential distribution is what ties the gap description to the independent-increments description: the process cannot remember when the last event occurred.

sections.title: Arrival times are uniform given the count

blocks.x: Given $N(t)=n$, the arrival times $(T_1,\dots,T_n)$ have the same joint law as the order statistics of $n$ i.i.d. $U(0,t)$ random variables. That is, the conditional joint density is $n!/t^n$ on $\{0<t_1<\dots<t_n<t\}$.

The joint density of $(T_1,\dots,T_n)$ follows from the change of variables $t_k=\tau_1+\dots+\tau_k$ (Jacobian $1$, triangular matrix) applied to the product density $\lambda^ne^{-\lambda(\tau_1+\dots+\tau_n)}$: it is $\lambda^ne^{-\lambda t_n}$ on $0<t_1<\dots<t_n$. The event $\{N(t)=n\}$ is $\{T_n\le t<T_{n+1}\}$, and $\Prob(T_{n+1}>t\given T_1,\dots,T_n)=e^{-\lambda(t-t_n)}$. So the joint density of the first $n$ arrival times and the event $\{N(t)=n\}$ is $\lambda^ne^{-\lambda t_n}e^{-\lambda(t-t_n)}=\lambda^ne^{-\lambda t}$ on $0<t_1<\dots<t_n<t$; it is constant. Dividing by $\Prob(N(t)=n)=e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^n/n!$ gives conditional density $n!/t^n$, which is the density of the order statistics of $n$ uniform points (the $n!$ orderings of $n$ i.i.d. uniform points all produce the same ordered vector).

This theorem says: once you know how many events occurred in $(0,t]$, their locations are like uniformly scattered points. It is the reason the Poisson process is called a model of “complete randomness”.

Customers arrive according to a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$ over $[0,t]$. The total waiting time until time $t$ of all customers who have arrived is $W=\sum_i(t-T_i)$. Given $N(t)=n$, each $t-T_i$ behaves like $U(0,t)$, so $\Exp[W\given N(t)=n]=nt/2$ and $\Exp[W]=\Exp[N(t)]t/2=\lambda t^2/2$.
If $N_1,N_2$ are independent Poisson processes with rates $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$, then $N_1+N_2$ is a Poisson process with rate $\lambda_1+\lambda_2$.

Independent and stationary increments are inherited from the two independent processes. For a fixed interval, $N_1(t)-N_1(s)$ and $N_2(t)-N_2(s)$ are independent Poisson variables, and the sum is Poisson with the sum of the parameters (Theorem 6.12(ii)). Counting a combined event at a time when both processes jump has probability zero.

Let $N$ be a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$, and suppose each event is independently of type 1 with probability $p$ and of type 2 with probability $q=1-p$. Let $N_1,N_2$ count the events of each type. Then $N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent Poisson processes of rates $\lambda p$ and $\lambda q$.
We verify the joint law of the counts in a fixed interval of length $t$. Given $N(t)=a+b$, the number of type-1 events is $\mathrm{Bin}(a+b,p)$, so

\Prob(N_1(t)=a,N_2(t)=b)=e^{-\lambda t}\frac{(\lambda t)^{a+b}}{(a+b)!}\binom{a+b}{a}p^aq^b
=\Bigl[e^{-\lambda pt}\frac{(\lambda pt)^a}{a!}\Bigr]\Bigl[e^{-\lambda qt}\frac{(\lambda qt)^b}{b!}\Bigr],

using $e^{-\lambda t}=e^{-\lambda pt}e^{-\lambda qt}$. The product form shows independence and the Poisson marginals. Independent increments of the thinned processes follow from the independent increments of $N$ and independent labelling.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: the independence in thinning is surprising and special

blocks.x: If a Poisson number of customers each buys with probability $p$, the numbers of buyers and non-buyers are independent. For a fixed (non-random) total $n$ they would be perfectly negatively correlated ($b=n-a$). The randomness of the total is exactly what restores independence. This characterises the Poisson law.

Two independent Poisson processes with rates $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ run in parallel. The first event of the superposition occurs at the minimum of two independent exponentials, and by Theorem 8.15 the first event comes from process 1 with probability $\lambda_1/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)$. After each event, by memorylessness, the race restarts. Hence the probability that process 1 gets $m$ events before process 2 gets $n$ is the probability that in a sequence of independent trials, each a success with probability $\lambda_1/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)$, we have at least $m$ successes in the first $m+n-1$ trials.

Buses arrive as a Poisson process with rate $\lambda=1/10$ per minute (mean gap $10$ minutes). You arrive at a fixed time $t$ far from the start. How long do you wait? By memorylessness the residual wait is $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$, with mean $10$ minutes (not $5$!). The time since the previous bus (the age) is $\min(\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda),t)$ (looking backwards, the process is again Poisson, truncated at time $0$), with mean $(1-e^{-\lambda t})/\lambda\to10$. The gap that contains your arrival time has length age plus residual:
\Exp[\text{length of the gap covering }t]=\frac{1-e^{-\lambda t}}\lambda+\frac1\lambda\xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{}\frac2\lambda=20\text{ minutes},
twice the average gap.

There is no contradiction: a random time is more likely to land in a long gap than in a short one, since long gaps cover more time. The gap seen from a randomly chosen time has the size-biased density $xf(x)/\Exp[\tau]$; for exponential gaps this is the Gamma$(2,\lambda)$ density, with mean $2/\lambda$. The same effect explains why your friends have more friends than you do on average, why classes seem larger than the university’s average class size, and why a random passenger finds the bus fuller than average.
Let $N$ be a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$ and $Y_1,Y_2,\dots$ i.i.d. and independent of $N$. The compound Poisson process is $X(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{N(t)}Y_i$.
By the random-sum formulas (Theorem 9.9) with $N(t)\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda t)$ (mean and variance both $\lambda t$),
\Exp[X(t)]=\lambda t\,\Exp[Y],\qquad\Var(X(t))=\lambda t\,\Exp[Y^2].

(Since $\Var(X(t))=\Exp[N]\Var(Y)+\Var(N)\Exp[Y]^2=\lambda t(\Var(Y)+\Exp[Y]^2)$.) This is the Cram'er–Lundberg model of insurance claims: premiums arrive at a constant rate, claims at Poisson times with random sizes.
A counting process with independent increments and $N(t)-N(s)\sim\mathrm{Poisson}\bigl(\int_s^t\lambda(u)\,du\bigr)$ is a non-homogeneous Poisson process with intensity function $\lambda(u)\ge0$.

It is obtained from a rate-$1$ Poisson process by the time change $\Lambda(t)=\int_0^t\lambda(u)\,du$ (that is, $N(t)=N_1(\Lambda(t))$), or by thinning a rate-$\lambda_{\max}$ process, accepting an event at time $u$ with probability $\lambda(u)/\lambda_{\max}$. The latter is also the standard simulation method (Chapter 17).

(1) Time to $n$th event: Gamma$(n,\lambda)$, mean $n/\lambda$. (2) Count in an interval: Poisson$(\lambda\times\text{length})$, and disjoint intervals are independent. (3) Two competing streams: superposition; the probability that stream $i$ goes first is $\lambda_i/\sum\lambda_j$. (4) Classification of events: thinning gives independent Poisson streams. (5) Given $n$ events in $[0,t]$: the times are i.i.d. uniform. (6) Time of arrival of a random observer: size-biased gap, mean $2/\lambda$.
Customers arrive at rate $6$ per hour. Find the probability that no one arrives in a $15$-minute interval, that at least $2$ arrive, and the expected time until the $5$th arrival.
Given exactly one event in $[0,t]$, show that its time is uniform on $[0,t]$.
Show that $\Cov(N(s),N(t))=\lambda\min(s,t)$.
Events of two independent Poisson processes of rates $2$ and $3$ are merged. What is the probability that the first $5$ events contain exactly $2$ of the first type?

A shop has two kinds of customers, arriving as independent Poisson processes with rates $3$ and $5$ per hour. Given that exactly $4$ customers arrived in the first hour, what is the probability that exactly $1$ was of the first type?
Let $X(t)$ be compound Poisson with $\lambda=2$ and claims uniform on $[0,1]$. Find the mean and variance of $X(5)$.
Prove that $T_n/n\to1/\lambda$ almost surely as $n\to\infty$ and hence $N(t)/t\to\lambda$ almost surely as $t\to\infty$.
(Challenge) Derive the density of the length of the gap covering the fixed time $t$ for a Poisson process and verify that it converges to the Gamma$(2,\lambda)$ density as $t\to\infty$.
